record.paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
record.original_question: How should a federated optimization system choose the number of local client updates before aggregation, and potentially the aggregation rule itself, so that the resulting training process achieves the best wall-clock convergence rather than merely good iteration complexity?

evidence.quote: How then to chooseK? Performing more local updates at the clients will increase the divergence between the resulting local models at the clients, before they are averaged. ... The optimal number of local updates strikes a balance between these two phenomena and achieves the fastest error versus wallclock time convergence. ... However, it is unclear whether this aggregation method will result in the fastest error convergence.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a distributed optimization problem in which a central server seeks to minimize a global objective F(w) = (1/N) Σ_{i=1}^N F_i(w), where each F_i: R^d → R is a local objective held by client i, accessible only through stochastic gradient queries. Training proceeds in synchronous rounds: in round t the server broadcasts a model w_t to a subset S_t of clients; each client i ∈ S_t initializes w_{t,0}^{(i)} = w_t and performs K local stochastic gradient steps w_{t,k+1}^{(i)} = w_{t,k}^{(i)} − η ∇̂F_i(w_{t,k}^{(i)}); the server then aggregates the resulting local iterates via an aggregation rule A to form w_{t+1} = A({w_{t,K}^{(i)} : i ∈ S_t}). Each round incurs a wall-clock cost τ_round(K) = τ_compute · K + τ_communication, where τ_compute and τ_communication are positive constants modeling per-step local computation time and per-round communication time, respectively. Increasing K reduces the number of communication rounds but increases the divergence between local iterates before aggregation, while decreasing K incurs more communication overhead.

Problem: Determine the choice of the local-step count K (possibly varying with t) and of the aggregation rule A that minimizes the expected wall-clock time required to reach a target sub-optimality E[F(w_T)] − inf F ≤ ε, as opposed to merely minimizing the number of rounds T or the iteration complexity. In particular, characterize, under standard assumptions (e.g., L-smoothness of each F_i, bounded stochastic gradient variance, and a measure of client heterogeneity), the optimal K* = K*(τ_compute, τ_communication, ε, L, σ², heterogeneity) and identify whether simple averaging A(w^{(1)},…,w^{(n)}) = (1/n) Σ w^{(i)} is wall-clock optimal, or whether some other aggregation rule yields strictly faster wall-clock convergence.
artifact.status_search_result: The question of optimally trading local computation against communication for wall-clock convergence in federated/local-SGD style optimization, and whether simple averaging is the wall-clock optimal aggregation rule, remains an active research area. While numerous works (e.g., Local SGD analyses by Stich, Khaled–Mishchenko–Richtárik, FedAvg convergence by Li et al., FedNova by Wang et al., SCAFFOLD by Karimireddy et al.) provide upper bounds and adaptive schemes for choosing K under various heterogeneity assumptions, no general closed-form characterization of the wall-clock-optimal K and aggregation rule has been established. The problem is generally regarded as open.

status_evidence.title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
status_evidence.snippet: The optimal number of local updates strikes a balance ... However, it is unclear whether this aggregation method will result in the fastest error convergence.
status_evidence.claim: The choice of K and aggregation rule for wall-clock optimality is posed as open.

status_evidence.title: Tackling the Objective Inconsistency Problem in Heterogeneous Federated Optimization (FedNova)
status_evidence.snippet: We propose a normalized averaging method (FedNova) that eliminates objective inconsistency while preserving fast error convergence.
status_evidence.claim: Subsequent work proposes alternative aggregation rules but does not establish wall-clock optimality.

status_evidence.title: SCAFFOLD: Stochastic Controlled Averaging for Federated Learning
status_evidence.snippet: SCAFFOLD uses control variates to correct for client drift in local updates.
status_evidence.claim: Variance-reduced aggregation improves iteration complexity but optimal K vs. wall-clock remains unsettled.
